Our editorial process produces two outputs: (i) public reviews designed to be posted alongside the preprint for the benefit of readers; (ii) feedback on the manuscript for the authors, including requests for revisions, shown below. We also include an acceptance summary that explains what the editors found interesting or important about the work.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Zebrafish caudal fin amputation induces a metabolic switch necessary for cell identity transitions and cell cycle re-entry to support blastema formation and bone regeneration" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by Phillip Newmark as Reviewing Editor and Didier Stainier as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Yi Feng (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) One of the major claims of the manuscript is that there is a "metabolic switch" from OXPHOS to aerobic glycolysis. The authors clearly show that enhanced glycolysis is indispensable for osteoblast dedifferentiation and cell cycle reentry during regeneration; however, they do not provide direct evidence that OXPHOS is diminished. Although treatment with two OXPHOS inhibitors (MB6, UK5099) does not inhibit regeneration, the authors provide no rationale or citations for the concentrations of the drugs used here, nor validation that these concentrations are effective in the animal. Thus, for the authors to maintain their assertion of a "metabolic switch," they should provide further evidence to support the downregulation of OXPHOS (e.g., is PDK upregulated? Is mitochondria pyruvate carrier downregulated? Are TCA cycle intermediates downregulated?). In the absence of such additional support for OXPHOS downregulation, the authors should modify their text (title, abstract, and main manuscript) and tone down their conclusions accordingly.

2) In the course of our editorial consultation, one reviewer noted that if UK5099 treatment blocks pyruvate entry into mitochondria, it should lead to enhanced lactate production. Based on the authors' model, enhanced lactate might be predicted to enhance regeneration. Figure 3S shows a slightly increased blastema area in UK5099-treated animals, but the sample size is quite small (n=5). The authors are encouraged to repeat this experiment and increase their sample sizes.

3) In their comments (included below), reviewer #1 noted that the terminology used in this manuscript to define proximal and distal blastema, as well as the patterning zone is not consistent with standard usage in the field. The figures and text should be modified so that use of these terms is consistent with standard usage. The authors should also comment on why they appear to be detecting proliferation in the distal blastema (Figures 6H, S6A-C), in contrast to previous reports.

4) As requested by Reviewer #2 in their public review, please provide more details of the microarray analysis reported in Figure S1, along with documentation of the differentially expressed genes, including annotations, fold changes, and p values.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

1. Positive impact of glycolysis activation or oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) inhibition

The authors nicely demonstrate the negative impact of glycolysis inhibition on fin regeneration and its cellular mechanisms, such as dedifferentiation, blastema formation and proliferation. However, the authors did not address another important aspect whether activation of glycolysis or inhibition of OXPHOS can enhance regeneration. One can argue that glycolysis is an essential metabolism and thus inhibition of glycolysis may cause defects of any biological events, including regeneration. Thus, another important approach is to determine whether metabolic reprogramming can enhance the regenerative program. I understand that the authors tried to address this by targeting OXPHOS but OXPHOS enzymes do not show differential transcription and UK5099 and MB6 do not impact fin regeneration. To address this further, I recommend the following:

1) LC-MS analysis

It is unclear whether the authors target to profile only four metabolites with LC-MS analysis (Figure 2E). I expect that the authors may be able to get more data from LC-MS, such as a profile of TCA cycle intermediates and key metabolites (succinate, citrate, malate, and so on). Even, there are more glucose metabolites, such as glucose-6-phosphate, fructose 6-phosphate, and so on. As the authors focus on glycolysis and OXPHOS, the profiles of more glycolysis and TCA cycle metabolite changes should be provided.

2) Functional impact of glycolysis activation and/or OXPHOS inhibition

The authors used two drugs, MB6 and UK5099. However, it is unclear whether treatment of these drugs can efficiently and specifically inhibit OXPHOS. By brief literature search, it is hard to find out papers using these two drugs with animals (although there are multiple papers treating these drugs with cells). Thus, I recommend alternative approaches.

a) Genetic method

Fukuda et al., (2020, EMBO reports, DOI 10.15252/embr.201949752) employed genetic manipulation to enhance glycolysis in adult zebrafish. They used ppargc1a mutants and pdk3b overexpression line, providing evidence that metabolic switch can result in positive effects of heart regeneration. Magadum et al., (2020, Circulation, DOI: 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.119.043067) also used mouse genetics to transiently express Pkm2 and demonstrated positive effects on heart regeneration. Note that pkm2 is a well-characterized glycolytic enzyme in cancer that promotes glucose metabolism toward lactate. Based on Fukuda's work, pkma2 is likely a homolog of pkm2 in zebrafish. The authors consider using one of these animal models to determine whether metabolic reprogramming can enhance fin regeneration.

b) Pharmaceutical approach

An alternative approach is to change metabolism by treating drugs. Bae et al., (2021, Circulation, DOI: 10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.120.049952) changed mouse metabolism by treating several drugs. They inhibit the succinate dehydrogenase enzyme complex by treating malonate and Atpenin A5 in mice. The authors consider treating these drugs and assess whether the metabolic switch can enhance fin regeneration.

2. Blastema subdivision

The blastema is defined as a proliferative cell mass, indicating that there are dedifferentiated cells, and once cells exit blastema they differentiate. In a 2002 paper (Nechiporuk and Keating, Development), the authors identified there are two distinct populations in the blastema. Distally located blastema cells are non-proliferative but express blastema marker msxb, naming it as distal blastema (DB). Thereafter, this DB is similarly used by multiple groups in the fin regeneration field as shown by several papers (Kang et al., Dev. Cell, 2013; Wehner et al., Cell Reports, 2014). This DB is a very small domain at the tip of mesenchymal cells. Based on previous works (Wehner et al., Cell Reports, 2014 and Stewart et al., Cell Reports, 2014), this DB is not marked by runx2 positive cell lining. By contrast, proximal blastema (PB) contains bilateral zones of proliferative pre-OB runx2 positive cell layers. As PB is a major blastema region and comprises proliferative cells, the PB ends by emerging differentiated cells, such as osterix positive cells. As patterning zone (PZ) indicates differentiation, the PZ area starts with osx expressing cells. This compartmentalization of blastema is standard in fin regeneration. However, the authors define DB, PB, and PZ incorrectly. In Figure 6B, DB actually indicates PB and both PB and PZ indicate PZ. DB is a very small domain distal to PB, which is not annotated in Figure 6B. Thus, Figure 6 and Sup Figure 5 use incorrect indications and result 5 "Glycolysis suppression leads to ~" is also incorrectly described.

Line 321 "show cycling Runx2+ pre-OBs maintain the progenitor pool in the DB"

– This is not DB, but PB.

Line 322" as they proliferate and populate the PB, they differentiate into fast-proliferating Runx2+ Osx+ immature OBs"

– This describes PZ, not PB (or the border of PB and PZ as it is not possible to clearly subdivide these two regions).

I highly recommend revising the manuscript (result section 5 and discussion) and figures based on the definition of PB and DB widely used in the field.

3. Long-term effects of glycolysis inhibition

The authors assess fin regeneration before 48hpa. How about after 48 hours? Are there any bone phenotypes at 4 or 7 dpa or is bone completely lost?

4. Effect of glycolysis inhibition on uninjured fins (homeostasis)

Is there any outcome on OB behavior or fin integrity from blocking glycolysis (with 2DG) in uninjured fins?

claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed increase in ldha expression shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Dedifferentiating osteoblasts change their metabolic signature, adopting a metabolic program that increases glycolysis.
claims.source: These data suggest that dedifferentiating OBs change their metabolic signature, adopting a metabolic program that increases glycolysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptomic data showing upregulation of glycolytic enzymes and ldha.

claims.claim: Osteoblasts account for around 1-3% of the total cell number in a bony-ray segment.
claims.source: Since OBs only account for around 1–3% of the total cell number in a bony-ray segment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: At 6 hpa, most glycolytic enzymes were highly upregulated in the whole fin stump, including hk1, hk2, pfkpa, and pyruvate kinase (pkma).
claims.source: At 6 hpa, when cells start to dedifferentiate, most glycolytic enzymes were highly upregulated, including hk1, hk2, pfkpa, and pyruvate kinase (pkma) (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: At 6 hpa, ldha expression was increased in the whole fin stump.
claims.source: Importantly, as observed during OB dedifferentiation, ldha expression was increased and pyruvate dehydrogenase a 1b (pdha1b) was downregulated.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: At 6 hpa, pyruvate dehydrogenase a 1b (pdha1b) was downregulated in the whole fin stump.
claims.source: Importantly, as observed during OB dedifferentiation, ldha expression was increased and pyruvate dehydrogenase a 1b (pdha1b) was downregulated.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Pdha1b is part of the Pdh1 complex, which catalyzes irreversibly the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA.
claims.source: pdha1b is part of the Pdh1 complex, which catalyzes irreversibly the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and progression to OXPHOS
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established biochemical knowledge about the Pdh1 complex.

claims.claim: The downregulation of pdha1b corroborates that at 6 hpa pyruvate is being shunt from the mitochondria and stimulating lactate-producing glycolysis.
claims.source: pdha1b is part of the Pdh1 complex, which catalyzes irreversibly the conversion of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA and progression to OXPHOS, further corroborating that at this stage pyruvate is being shunt from the mitochondria and stimulating lactate-producing glycolysis (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed downregulation of pdha1b shown in Figure 2C, combined with knowledge of its biochemical function.

claims.claim: At 6 hpa, most OXPHOS components analyzed remained unchanged or slightly upregulated in the whole fin stump.
claims.source: As for the OXPHOS components analyzed, most remained unchanged or slightly upregulated. However, this increase in expression was not as accentuated as the one observed for the glycolytic pathway (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, most glycolytic enzymes were still significantly upregulated in the whole fin stump, although not as striking as at 6 hpa.
claims.source: Later, at 24 hpa, when most cells have dedifferentiated and the blastema starts to be assembled, we observed that most glycolytic enzymes were still significantly upregulated, although not as striking as at 6 hpa time-point, and ldha expression continued to be upregulated (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, ldha expression continued to be upregulated in the whole fin stump.
claims.source: Later, at 24 hpa, when most cells have dedifferentiated and the blastema starts to be assembled, we observed that most glycolytic enzymes were still significantly upregulated, although not as striking as at 6 hpa time-point, and ldha expression continued to be upregulated (Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, there is an increase in expression of some OXPHOS components in the whole fin stump.
claims.source: At this time-point, we also observed an increase in expression of some OXPHOS components (Figure 2D), suggesting that blastema formation may also require mitochondrial glucose oxidation.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Blastema formation may also require mitochondrial glucose oxidation.
claims.source: At this time-point, we also observed an increase in expression of some OXPHOS components (Figure 2D), suggesting that blastema formation may also require mitochondrial glucose oxidation.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed increase in OXPHOS component expression at 24 hpa shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Consistent upregulation of genes associated with glycolysis and lactate production suggests that the osteoblast dedifferentiation process and possibly the early response to amputation are characterized by a metabolic adaptation toward glycolysis.
claims.source: Consistent upregulation of the genes associated with glycolysis and lactate production suggests that the OB dedifferentiation process and possibly the early response to amputation are characterized by a metabolic adaptation toward glycolysis.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the consistent upregulation of glycolytic genes observed in the data.

claims.claim: There is an increase in glucose at 6 and 24 hpa in relation to control fins (0 hpa).
claims.source: According with our transcriptome data, we observed an increase in glucose and lactate at 6 and 24 hpa in relation to control fins (0 hpa), which is consistent with an increment in the glycolytic influx (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: There is an increase in lactate at 6 and 24 hpa in relation to control fins (0 hpa).
claims.source: According with our transcriptome data, we observed an increase in glucose and lactate at 6 and 24 hpa in relation to control fins (0 hpa), which is consistent with an increment in the glycolytic influx (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: The increase in glucose and lactate at 6 and 24 hpa is consistent with an increment in the glycolytic influx.
claims.source: According with our transcriptome data, we observed an increase in glucose and lactate at 6 and 24 hpa in relation to control fins (0 hpa), which is consistent with an increment in the glycolytic influx (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the metabolite measurements shown in Figure 2E, combined with the transcriptome data.

claims.claim: There is a strong increase of glutamine and glutamate at 24 hpa but not at 6 hpa.
claims.source: We also observed a strong increase of glutamine and glutamate at 24 hpa but not at 6 hpa (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: Glutamine and glutamate act as important substrates for protein and nucleotide synthesis necessary to support cellular integrity and growth.
claims.source: Glutamine and glutamate act as important substrates for protein and nucleotide synthesis necessary to support cellular integrity and growth suggesting an increase in biosynthesis (Newsholme et al., 2003; Yoo et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Newsholme et al., 2003; Yoo et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The increase in glutamine and glutamate at 24 hpa suggests an increase in biosynthesis.
claims.source: Glutamine and glutamate act as important substrates for protein and nucleotide synthesis necessary to support cellular integrity and growth suggesting an increase in biosynthesis (Newsholme et al., 2003; Yoo et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed increase in glutamine and glutamate at 24 hpa, combined with knowledge of their biochemical roles (Newsholme et al., 2003; Yoo et al., 2020).

claims.claim: In control fins (0 hpa), glucose uptake is detected in the intersegment region.
claims.source: In control fins (0 hpa), we detected glucose uptake in the intersegment region (Figure 2F–H arrows,L,N)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 2-NBDG uptake imaging data shown in Figure 2F-H, L, N.

claims.claim: A population of osteoblast progenitors have been identified in the intersegment region.
claims.source: In control fins (0 hpa), we detected glucose uptake in the intersegment region (Figure 2F–H arrows,L,N), where a population of OP have been identified (Ando et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Ando et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Under homeostatic conditions, osteoblast progenitor cells in the intersegment region may require higher levels of glucose to maintain the progenitor niche.
claims.source: In control fins (0 hpa), we detected glucose uptake in the intersegment region (Figure 2F–H arrows,L,N), where a population of OP have been identified (Ando et al., 2017), which may imply that under homeostatic conditions, these cells require higher levels of glucose to maintain the progenitor niche.
claims.evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the observed glucose uptake in the intersegment region shown in Figure 2F-H, L, N, combined with knowledge of the OP population (Ando et al., 2017).

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, there is a significant increase of glucose uptake in the blastema primordium and in the first segment below the amputation.
claims.source: At 24 hpa, we observed a significant increase of glucose uptake in the blastema primordium and in the first segment below the amputation (Figure 2I–K, M and N).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by 2-NBDG uptake imaging data shown in Figure 2I-K, M and N.

claims.claim: There is an increase in expression of genes associated with mitochondrial fission, namely drp1 and fis1, at 6 hpa but not at 24 hpa, when compared to uninjured condition (0 hpa).
claims.source: By performing a qPCR analysis at 0, 6, and 24 hpa, we observed an increase in expression of genes associated with mitochondrial fission, namely drp1 and fis1, at 6 hpa but not at 24 hpa, when compared to uninjured condition (0 hpa) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: There is an increase in the number of mitochondria per cell at 6 and 24 hpa, in relation to uninjured control.
claims.source: By quantifying the number of mitochondria using the reporter line MLS-GFP, which labels the mitochondria membrane (Kim et al., 2008), we noticed an increase in the number of mitochondria per cell at 6 and 24 hpa, in relation to uninjured control (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H',I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of mitochondria using the MLS-GFP reporter line shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H',I.

claims.claim: There is a significant increase in percentage of mitochondria smaller than 0.1 µm³ at 6 hpa.
claims.source: In accordance with an increase in mitochondria fission, we observed a significant increase in percentage of mitochondria smaller than 0,1 µm3 at 6 hpa, while at 24 hpa the mitochondria size profile is similar to the 0 hpa condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H',J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondria volume measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H',J.

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, the mitochondria size profile is similar to the 0 hpa condition.
claims.source: In accordance with an increase in mitochondria fission, we observed a significant increase in percentage of mitochondria smaller than 0,1 µm3 at 6 hpa, while at 24 hpa the mitochondria size profile is similar to the 0 hpa condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H',J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by mitochondria volume measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C-H',J.

claims.claim: The early stages of regeneration involve an upregulation of glycolytic activity, which is accompanied by a temporally restricted program of mitochondria fission.
claims.source: Taken together, these results are in consistent with an increase in mitochondrial fission triggered by amputation and further supports the hypothesis that the early stages of regeneration involve an upregulation of glycolytic activity, which is accompanied by a temporally restricted program of mitochondria fission.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on glycolytic gene expression, metabolite levels, and mitochondrial fission.

claims.claim: Metabolic adaptation enhancing glycolysis seems to constitute an integral response to amputation, tightly regulated in terms of time and space.
claims.source: Thus, metabolic adaptation enhancing glycolysis seems to constitute an integral response to amputation, tightly regulated in terms of time and space.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the section.

claims.claim: Cells respond to injury by increasing the glycolytic influx, lactate production and mitochondrial fission just preceding dedifferentiation and blastema formation.
claims.source: Our transcriptome and metabolome studies indicate a specific metabolic signature as part of an early response to amputation by OBs and by the remaining caudal fin tissue. Overall, cells respond to injury by increasing the glycolytic influx, lactate production and mitochondrial fission just preceding dedifferentiation and blastema formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the transcriptome and metabolome data presented in the section.

claims.claim: Amputation induces a reprogramming of the metabolic profile.
claims.source: These results corroborate the hypothesis that amputation induces a reprogramming of the metabolic profile, which may be part of a general program that coordinates the regenerative response.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the section.

claims.claim: The blastema is a hallmark and prerequisite of epimorphic regeneration.
claims.source: The blastema is a hallmark and prerequisite of epimorphic regeneration and is fully assembled within 48 hpa (Kawakami, 2010; Poss et al., 2003; Pfefferli and Jaźwińska, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kawakami, 2010; Poss et al., 2003; Pfefferli and Jaźwińska, 2015).

claims.claim: The blastema is fully assembled within 48 hpa.
claims.source: The blastema is a hallmark and prerequisite of epimorphic regeneration and is fully assembled within 48 hpa (Kawakami, 2010; Poss et al., 2003; Pfefferli and Jaźwińska, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kawakami, 2010; Poss et al., 2003; Pfefferli and Jaźwińska, 2015).

claims.claim: 2-Deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) competes with glucose for hexokinase catalytic domain, inhibiting the downstream products derived from glucose.
claims.source: Firstly, we inhibited glycolysis using an established glucose analogue, 2-Deoxy-D-glucose (2DG) (Sinclair et al., 2021; Honkoop et al., 2019), that competes with glucose for Hk catalytic domain, the first step of glycolysis, inhibiting the downstream products derived from glucose.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Sinclair et al., 2021; Honkoop et al., 2019) and describes the mechanism of action of 2DG.

claims.claim: The higher the duration of 2DG treatment, the stronger the effect on blastema growth in comparison to control fins.
claims.source: We observed that the higher the duration of the treatment the stronger the effect on blastema growth in comparison to control fins (Figure 3C and D–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3C and D-K.

claims.claim: A single dose of 2DG administered at 0 hpa showed significant smaller regenerates when compared to control fins.
claims.source: Interestingly, a single dose of 2DG administered at 0 hpa already showed significant smaller regenerates when compared to control fins (Figure 3C–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3C-E.

claims.claim: Administration of 2DG between 0-12, 0-24, and 0-36 hpa had a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on the overall regenerated area.
claims.source: Administration of 2DG between 0–12, 0–24, and 0–36 hpa had a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on the overall regenerated area (Figure 3C and F–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3C and F-K.

claims.claim: Blocking of the glycolytic influx for the first 36 hpa led to a complete abrogation of blastema assembly.
claims.source: Accordingly, blocking of the glycolytic influx for the first 36 hpa led to a complete abrogation of blastema assembly (Figure 3C and J–K).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area and images shown in Figure 3C and J-K.

claims.claim: The glycolysis inhibitor 3-(3-pyridinyl)-1-(4-pyridinyl)-2-propen-1-one (3PO) exhibited a general impairment of caudal fin regeneration at 48 hpa in relation to control fins.
claims.source: Similarly, the glycolysis inhibitor acting downstream of 2DG, 3-(3-pyridinyl)–1-(4-pyridinyl)–2-propen-1-one (3PO), which partially inhibits the glycolytic activator of Pfk (Schoors et al., 2014 Figure 3A), also exhibited a general impairment of caudal fin regeneration, as observed at 48 hpa in relation to control fins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D and citation to a previous study (Schoors et al., 2014).

claims.claim: 3PO partially inhibits the glycolytic activator of phosphofructokinase (Pfk).
claims.source: Similarly, the glycolysis inhibitor acting downstream of 2DG, 3-(3-pyridinyl)–1-(4-pyridinyl)–2-propen-1-one (3PO), which partially inhibits the glycolytic activator of Pfk (Schoors et al., 2014 Figure 3A)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study (Schoors et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Sodium Oxamate (S.O.) administration during the first 36 hpa resulted in a decrease of the caudal fin regenerated area in respect to control caudal fins.
claims.source: S.O. administration during the first 36 hpa resulted in a decrease of the caudal fin regenerated area in respect to control caudal fins (Figure 3L–O), although exhibiting a milder effect when compared to glycolysis inhibition (Figure 3C–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3L-O.

claims.claim: Sodium Oxamate (S.O.) exhibited a milder effect on regeneration when compared to glycolysis inhibition.
claims.source: S.O. administration during the first 36 hpa resulted in a decrease of the caudal fin regenerated area in respect to control caudal fins (Figure 3L–O), although exhibiting a milder effect when compared to glycolysis inhibition (Figure 3C–K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-D).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of quantification data shown in Figure 3L-O and Figure 3C-K.

claims.claim: Inhibition of OXPHOS using a mitochondrial pyruvate carrier inhibitor (UK5099) led to a mild, although significant, increase in the regenerated area at 48 hpa when compared to control fins.
claims.source: In contrast, inhibition of OXPHOS using a mitochondrial pyruvate carrier inhibitor (UK5099) (Hildyard et al., 2005; Figure 3A) led to a mild, although significant, increase in the regenerated area at 48 hpa when compared to control fins (Figure 3P-S), suggesting an improvement of the regenerative ability.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3P-S and citation to a previous study (Hildyard et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Inhibition of OXPHOS using UK5099 suggests an improvement of the regenerative ability.
claims.source: In contrast, inhibition of OXPHOS using a mitochondrial pyruvate carrier inhibitor (UK5099) (Hildyard et al., 2005; Figure 3A) led to a mild, although significant, increase in the regenerated area at 48 hpa when compared to control fins (Figure 3P-S), suggesting an improvement of the regenerative ability.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed increase in regenerated area shown in Figure 3P-S.

claims.claim: The same effect was not observed using an inhibitor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (MitoBlock-6 (MB6)).
claims.source: The same effect was not observed using an inhibitor of the mitochondrial electron transport chain (MitoBlock-6 (MB6)) (Dabir et al., 2013; Figure 3A; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-H).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of regenerated area shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E-H and citation to a previous study (Dabir et al., 2013).

claims.claim: Glycolysis and lactate generation, but not OXPHOS, are essential for the initial stages of caudal fin regeneration.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that glycolysis and lactate generation, but not OXPHOS, are essential for the initial stages of caudal fin regeneration.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the pharmacological manipulation experiments presented in the section.

claims.claim: Cells that respond to amputation reprogram their metabolic profile to stimulate the glycolytic machinery/influx to support blastema formation.
claims.source: Our data strongly supports the hypothesis that the cells that respond to amputation reprogram their metabolic profile since very early thereby stimulating the glycolytic machinery/influx to support blastema formation.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the section.

claims.claim: Inhibition of the glycolytic influx led to a significant upregulation of bglap at 24 hpa.
claims.source: We observed that inhibition of the glycolytic influx led to a significant upregulation of bglap and to a decrease in both runx2 orthologues (Figure 4C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Inhibition of the glycolytic influx led to a decrease in both runx2 orthologues at 24 hpa.
claims.source: We observed that inhibition of the glycolytic influx led to a significant upregulation of bglap and to a decrease in both runx2 orthologues (Figure 4C)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: 2DG treatment had no effect on the number of dedifferentiated Runx2+Bglap+ pre-osteoblasts at 24 hpa.
claims.source: Immunofluorescence analysis for Runx2 in bglap:EGFP reporter fish, showed that 2DG treatment had no effect in the number of dedifferentiated Runx2 +Bglap + pre-OBs (Figure 4D–G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claims.claim: The number of Runx2+Bglap- pre-osteoblasts was significantly reduced upon 2DG treatment at 24 hpa when compared to control fins.
claims.source: However, the number of Runx2 +Bglap- pre-OBs was significantly reduced (Figure 4E–G) when compared to control fins (Figure 4D, F and G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence quantification data shown in Figure 4D-G.

claims.claim: Blocking glycolytic influx hampers mature osteoblast dedifferentiation, which become unable to operate as a source of pre-osteoblasts resulting in impaired pre-osteoblast pool assembly within the blastema primordium.
claims.source: Overall, these data indicate that blocking glycolytic influx hampers mature OB dedifferentiation, which become unable to operate as a source of pre-OB resulting in impaired pre-OB pool assembly within the blastema primordium.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data presented in the section.

claims.claim: During homeostasis, NF-kB pathway maintains retinoic acid (RA) signalling in osteoblasts, supporting differentiation.
claims.source: During homeostasis NF-kB pathway maintains retinoic acid (RA) signalling in OBs, supporting differentiation.
claims.evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the NF-kB-RA axis in osteoblast differentiation.

claims.claim: Upon amputation, NF-kB pathway becomes inactivated and RA is degraded through activity of the RA-degrading enzyme, Cyp26b1, thereby inducing osteoblast dedifferentiation.
claims.source: Upon amputation, NF-kB pathway becomes inactivated and RA is degraded through activity of the RA-degrading enzyme, Cyp26b1, thereby inducing OB dedifferentiation (Mishra et al., 2020; Blum and Begemann, 2015; Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Mishra et al., 2020; Blum and Begemann, 2015) and illustrated in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Bmp signaling is considered to be a potent inducer of osteoblast differentiation during regeneration.
claims.source: In addition, Bmp signaling is also considered to be a potent inducer of OB differentiation during regeneration (Stewart et al., 2014; Brandão et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2006; Quint et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Stewart et al., 2014; Brandão et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2006; Quint et al., 2002).

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, there is an increase in NF-kB target genes (nfkbiaa and nfkbiab) in 2DG-treated fins.
claims.source: We observed an increase in NF-kB target genes and in bmp2b, accompanied by a decrease in cyp26b1 in 2DG-treated fins.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, there is an increase in bmp2b in 2DG-treated fins.
claims.source: We observed an increase in NF-kB target genes and in bmp2b, accompanied by a decrease in cyp26b1 in 2DG-treated fins.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: At 24 hpa, there is a decrease in cyp26b1 in 2DG-treated fins.
claims.source: We observed an increase in NF-kB target genes and in bmp2b, accompanied by a decrease in cyp26b1 in 2DG-treated fins.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Suppression of glycolysis seems to maintain the mature osteoblast differentiation profile and to prevent their dedifferentiation after amputation, resembling a pre-amputation scenario.
claims.source: Thus, suppression of glycolysis seems to maintain the mature OB differentiation profile and to prevent their dedifferentiation after amputation, resembling a pre-amputation scenario.
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed gene expression changes upon 2DG treatment shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: 2DG administration had no effect on the ability of osteoblasts to migrate and reach the amputation zone at 24 hpa.
claims.source: Surprisingly, by measuring the relative cell displacement of the OB population in the first segment below the amputation region after 24 hpa, we observed that 2DG administration had no effect on the ability of OB to migrate and reach the amputation zone (Figure 5A–E).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by live-imaging quantification data shown in Figure 5A-E.

claims.claim: Cell cycle re-entry was strongly affected by 2DG treatment at 24 hpa.
claims.source: However, cell cycle re-entry, examined through a EdU 3 hr pulse assay in bglap:EGFP transgenics, was strongly affected by 2DG treatment (Figure 5F–G') contrasting with control caudal fins.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 5F-G'.

claims.claim: There is a significant reduction of total number of Runx2+Bglap+EdU+ pre-osteoblasts per area upon 2DG treatment at 24 hpa.
claims.source: We observed a significant reduction of total number of Runx2 +Bglap + EdU +pre OBs per area (Figure 5H) and percentage of Runx2 +Bglap + EdU +within the Runx2 +Bglap + population (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling quantification data shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: There is a significant reduction in the percentage of Runx2+Bglap+EdU+ within the Runx2+Bglap+ population upon 2DG treatment at 24 hpa.
claims.source: We observed a significant reduction of total number of Runx2 +Bglap + EdU +pre OBs per area (Figure 5H) and percentage of Runx2 +Bglap + EdU +within the Runx2 +Bglap + population (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling quantification data shown in Figure 5I.

claims.claim: There is a reduction in the number and relative percentage of Runx2+Bglap-EdU+ pre-osteoblasts upon 2DG treatment at 24 hpa.
claims.source: By quantifying the remaining pre-OB population Runx2 +Bglap-, we also observed a reduction in the number and relative percentage of Runx2 +Bglap-EdU+pre OBs upon 2DG treatment (Figure 5F–G' arrows, H,I).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling quantification data shown in Figure 5F-G', H, I.

claims.claim: Blocking glycolytic machinery has a severe impact on the number of pre-osteoblasts that re-enter the cell cycle, reducing their proliferative capacity.
claims.source: This indicates that blocking glycolytic machinery has a severe impact in the number of pre-OB that re-enter the cell cycle, reducing their proliferative capacity.
claims.evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on the EdU labeling data presented in the section.

claims.claim: Inhibition of cell cycle re-entry by 2DG was also observed in the blastema primordium mesenchyme at 24 hpa.
claims.source: This inhibition of cell cycle re-entry by 2DG was also observed in the blastema primordium mesenchyme (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F,H) and the overlying epidermal cap (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F,H.

claims.claim: Inhibition of cell cycle re-entry by 2DG was also observed in the overlying epidermal cap at 24 hpa.
claims.source: This inhibition of cell cycle re-entry by 2DG was also observed in the blastema primordium mesenchyme (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F,H) and the overlying epidermal cap (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F,G).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by EdU labeling quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-F,G.

claims.claim: There is a downregulation of wnt10a, igf2b and fgf20a in 2DG-treated caudal fins at 24 hpa in comparison to controls.
claims.source: This is predicted based on our results showing a downregulation of wnt10a, igf2b and fgf20a in 2DG-treated caudal fins in comparison to controls (Figure 5J).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5J.

claims.claim: The decline in the capacity of pre-osteoblasts to re-enter the cell cycle and to proliferate could be correlated with defects in the activity of Wnt, Insulin and Fgf signaling pathways.
claims.source: Moreover, the decline in the capacity of pre-OB to re-enter the cell cycle and to proliferate could be correlated with defects in the activity of pathways known to be indispensable for blastema proliferation, such as, Wnt, Insulin and Fgf signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2005; Poss et al., 2000; Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007; Chablais and Jazwinska, 2010; Wehner and Weidinger, 2015; Shibata et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed downregulation of wnt10a, igf2b and fgf20a, combined with citations to previous studies (Lee et al., 2005; Poss et al., 2000; Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007; Chablais and Jazwinska, 2010; Wehner and Weidinger, 2015; Shibata et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Wnt, Insulin and Fgf signaling pathways are indispensable for blastema proliferation.
claims.source: Moreover, the decline in the capacity of pre-OB to re-enter the cell cycle and to proliferate could be correlated with defects in the activity of pathways known to be indispensable for blastema proliferation, such as, Wnt, Insulin and Fgf signaling pathways (Lee et al., 2005; Poss et al., 2000; Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007; Chablais and Jazwinska, 2010; Wehner and Weidinger, 2015; Shibata et al., 2016).

results.result: Osteoblast dedifferentiation occurs earlier than previously reported, beginning at 6 hpa and continuing through 24 hpa. This process involves downregulation of mature markers (bglap), upregulation of pre-osteoblast markers (runx2), cell migration, cell cycle re-entry, and formation of a pre-osteoblast pool that incorporates into the blastema. Multiple osteoblast sources, including mature osteoblasts and potentially joint-associated progenitors, contribute to the pre-osteoblast pool.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C33 provide converging evidence from multiple experimental approaches (qPCR, live imaging, immunofluorescence) showing that osteoblast dedifferentiation begins at 6 hpa, earlier than the 12-24 hpa window reported in prior studies (C1-C2). The data demonstrate transcriptional changes (C7-C9), cell migration (C10-C12), cell cycle re-entry (C13-C14), and changes in marker expression (C15-C25) that collectively support the conclusion that dedifferentiation is an early response occurring during the wound healing phase (C29-C33).

results.result: At 6 hpa, osteoblasts and the whole fin stump undergo a metabolic adaptation characterized by upregulation of glycolytic enzymes (hk1, hk2, pfkp, pkma) and ldha, downregulation of pdha1b, increased glucose and lactate levels, and increased mitochondrial fission. This metabolic shift toward glycolysis persists at 24 hpa and is accompanied by increased glucose uptake in the blastema primordium.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C74 provide comprehensive evidence from transcriptomics (C35-C44), qPCR (C46-C56), mass spectrometry (C57-C62), glucose uptake assays (C63-C66), and mitochondrial imaging (C67-C71) demonstrating a coordinated metabolic shift toward glycolysis at early stages of regeneration. The data are internally consistent across multiple experimental approaches and show both isolated osteoblasts and whole tissue exhibit this metabolic adaptation.

results.result: Glycolysis and lactate generation, but not OXPHOS, are essential for blastema formation during caudal fin regeneration. Pharmacological inhibition of glycolysis with 2DG or 3PO causes dose-dependent reduction in blastema size, with complete abrogation when glycolysis is blocked for the first 36 hpa. Inhibition of lactate production with sodium oxamate shows milder effects, while OXPHOS inhibition with UK5099 slightly improves regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C90 demonstrate through multiple pharmacological interventions (2DG, 3PO, S.O., UK5099, MB6) that glycolysis is specifically required for blastema formation. The dose-dependent effects (C78-C81), specificity of different inhibitors (C82-C88), and differential effects on glycolysis vs. OXPHOS (C86-C88) provide strong evidence that glycolysis, rather than OXPHOS, is the critical metabolic pathway for early regeneration.

results.result: Glycolysis inhibition with 2DG prevents osteoblast dedifferentiation by maintaining the mature osteoblast differentiation profile. At 24 hpa, 2DG treatment leads to upregulation of bglap, downregulation of runx2, increased NF-κB target genes and bmp2b, and decreased cyp26b1, resembling a pre-amputation scenario. The number of Runx2+Bglap- pre-osteoblasts is significantly reduced, while Runx2+Bglap+ cells remain unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C102 provide consistent evidence from qPCR (C91-C92, C99-C101) and immunofluorescence (C93-C94) showing that glycolysis inhibition prevents the transcriptional changes associated with dedifferentiation. The data demonstrate that blocking glycolysis maintains expression of differentiation markers and pathways (NF-κB-RA axis, Bmp signaling) that normally suppress dedifferentiation, providing mechanistic insight into how glycolysis regulates cell fate transitions.

results.result: Glycolysis is required for cell cycle re-entry but not for osteoblast migration or survival. 2DG treatment at 24 hpa does not affect osteoblast migration to the amputation zone but severely reduces the number and percentage of proliferating pre-osteoblasts (Runx2+Bglap+EdU+ and Runx2+Bglap-EdU+), as well as proliferation in the mesenchyme and epidermis. This is associated with downregulation of wnt10a, igf2b, and fgf20a. Cell death is only slightly increased in the mesenchyme, not in epidermis or pre-osteoblasts.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C121 demonstrate through live imaging (C103), EdU labeling (C104-C107), and TUNEL assays (C115-C117) that glycolysis specifically regulates cell cycle re-entry without affecting migration or survival. The data show consistent effects across multiple cell types (pre-osteoblasts, mesenchyme, epidermis) and link the proliferation defects to downregulation of key signaling pathways (Wnt, Insulin, Fgf) known to regulate blastema proliferation (C111-C113).

results.result: Prolonged glycolysis inhibition through 48 hpa severely disrupts blastema organization and osteoblast subtype distribution. 2DG treatment causes a marked decrease in Runx2+Osx+ immature osteoblasts while Runx2+Osx- pre-osteoblasts remain unchanged, leading to an imbalance in osteoblast populations. Both osteoblast subtypes show significantly reduced proliferation, with the effect being more profound at 48 hpa than at 24 hpa. Extended 2DG treatment through 7 dpa completely abolishes bone regeneration without affecting uninjured fin morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C152 provide comprehensive evidence from immunofluorescence (C126-C135), EdU labeling (C136-C140), and calcein staining (C147-C151) showing that glycolysis is required for proper blastema organization and osteoblast differentiation. The data demonstrate specific effects on osteoblast subtype distribution (C130-C134) and proliferation (C136-C140) that are consistent with the known hierarchical organization of the blastema. The lack of effect on uninjured fins (C148-C151) provides an important control showing specificity for regeneration.

results.result: The study provides the first molecular characterization of osteoblasts at 6 hpa, preceding the dedifferentiation stage. Transcriptomic analysis reveals that mature osteoblasts begin changing their transcriptome earlier than previously expected, with the first hours after amputation being crucial for transcriptional and phenotypic alterations leading to dedifferentiation. The study addresses early stages of fin regeneration that have been least investigated in prior work.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C162 establish the novelty and significance of the transcriptomic analysis. The comparison to prior work (C153) and the demonstration of early transcriptional changes (C154-C158) are supported by the ArrayXS data (C35-C39). The claims about addressing an understudied time window (C160-C162) are reasonable given that most prior studies focused on 24 hpa onwards.

results.result: Osteoblasts and other cell lineages respond to amputation by undergoing a metabolic adaptation that favors glycolysis. This metabolic shift occurs at 6 hpa, persists through 24 hpa, and is accompanied by increased mitochondrial fission. Glycolysis is indispensable for blastema formation and regeneration, with the timing of these metabolic changes being fundamental for regeneration initiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C170 synthesize the key findings from the metabolic characterization (C40-C74) and functional studies (C77-C90). The conclusions are well-supported by the experimental data showing metabolic changes at the transcriptional, protein, and metabolite levels, as well as the functional requirement demonstrated through pharmacological inhibition.

results.result: Early wound response signals, particularly ROS production, may trigger metabolic changes during regeneration. ROS are produced by epithelial cells upon damage and can activate HIF-1α, which promotes metabolic reprogramming toward glycolysis in other contexts.
results.evaluation: Claims C171-C176 are speculative and based on literature citations rather than experimental data from this study. While the hypothesis is reasonable given the known connections between ROS, HIF-1α, and glycolysis (C173-C175), no experiments were performed to test whether ROS production is necessary for glycolysis stimulation during fin regeneration (C176). This represents a plausible mechanism but requires future experimental validation.

results.result: Osteoblasts and other cell types respond to amputation by engaging metabolic routes that boost lactate-producing glycolysis instead of OXPHOS, thereby acquiring metabolic traits of stem cells. This parallels the metabolic preferences of embryonic and adult stem cells, which rely on glycolysis and undergo metabolic rewiring to increase OXPHOS upon differentiation. The metabolic switch during iPSC reprogramming occurs before expression of endogenous reprogramming factors, suggesting metabolic reprogramming is a cause rather than consequence of cell reprogramming.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C187 draw well-supported parallels between the metabolic changes observed in regenerating osteoblasts and established knowledge about stem cell metabolism (C178-C181) and cellular reprogramming (C186-C187). The comparison is justified by the experimental data showing glycolysis upregulation (C40-C74) and is strengthened by extensive literature citations documenting similar metabolic preferences in stem cells and during reprogramming.

results.result: The metabolic changes during fin regeneration share parallels with cancer metabolism, including preference for glycolysis (Warburg effect) and elevated glutamine/glutamate levels. Metabolome studies show 100- and 400-fold increases in glutamine and glutamate at 24 hpa. Lactate production contributes to blastema formation, as inhibition of pyruvate-to-lactate conversion causes defects in blastema formation, though milder than glycolysis inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C188-C199 draw appropriate parallels between regeneration and cancer metabolism based on the experimental data (C57-C62, C84-C85, C196-C197). The comparison to the Warburg effect is justified by the observed preference for glycolysis over OXPHOS. The dramatic increases in glutamine and glutamate (C60, C193) are supported by mass spectrometry data. The functional role of lactate is demonstrated by sodium oxamate experiments (C84-C85, C197), though the authors appropriately note that mechanisms require future study (C199).

results.result: Glycolysis is not required for mature osteoblast recruitment and motility, despite aerobic glycolysis being known to support cancer cell migration. The regulation of glucose metabolism alterations throughout regeneration without falling into tumorigenesis requires future investigation.
results.evaluation: Claim C201 is well-supported by the live imaging data showing no effect of 2DG on osteoblast migration (C103). This finding is notable because it contrasts with the known role of glycolysis in cancer cell migration (C200), demonstrating specificity in how glycolysis regulates different aspects of cell behavior during regeneration. Claim C202 is a reasonable suggestion for future research given the parallels with cancer metabolism.

results.result: Glycolysis has an instructive role in regulating osteoblast dedifferentiation and blastema proliferation. Blocking glycolysis leads to NF-κB signaling stimulation and decreased cyp26b1 expression, indicating that increased glycolytic activity precedes and is necessary for mature osteoblast reprogramming. Glycolysis promotes expression of fgf20a, igf2b, and wnt10a, which cooperate to induce blastema proliferation. Glycolysis is necessary through blastema formation to generate new osteoblasts and maintain proper balance between osteoblast subtypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C203-C219 synthesize the mechanistic findings linking glycolysis to specific signaling pathways. The connection to the NF-κB-RA axis (C205-C207) is supported by qPCR data (C99-C101). The link to Fgf signaling (C208-C215) is supported by gene expression data (C111) and literature on Fgf's role in blastema proliferation (C210-C213). The overall conclusion about glycolysis regulating osteoblast balance (C217-C219) is supported by the immunofluorescence data at 48 hpa (C130-C134).

results.result: Pre-osteoblasts can derive from multiple sources: mature osteoblasts and joint-associated osteoblast progenitors. Glycolysis inhibition leads to diminished pre-osteoblast numbers before blastema formation, but numbers return to normal after blastema formation, possibly due to joint progenitors replenishing the pre-osteoblast pool over time.
results.evaluation: Claim C220 is well-supported by literature (Ando et al., 2017). Claims C222-C223 present an interesting observation about pre-osteoblast number recovery, but the interpretation that joint progenitors compensate for the loss of mature osteoblast-derived pre-osteoblasts is speculative (C223). The authors appropriately acknowledge this as speculation and call for future work (C224). The hypothesis is plausible but lacks direct experimental evidence in this study.

results.result: This study provides the first evidence that metabolic adaptation toward glycolysis governs mature osteoblast dedifferentiation and blastema proliferation, mediated through glycolysis-driven changes in gene expression that uncouple dedifferentiation from proliferation. Metabolic rewiring toward glycolysis appears to be a conserved mechanism in regenerative organisms, as planarians, amphibians, and other zebrafish tissues (heart, embryonic tail) also show glycolysis dependence during regeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C225-C226 appropriately summarize the major findings of the study, which are well-supported by the experimental data. Claims C229-C237 draw appropriate parallels to other regenerative systems based on literature citations (Osuma et al., 2018; Alibardi, 2014; Varela-Rodríguez et al., 2020; Honkoop et al., 2019; Fukuda et al., 2020; Sinclair et al., 2021). The suggestion to examine hexosamine pathway function (C238) is a reasonable direction for future research given the findings in embryonic tail regeneration.

results.result: Mammals have poor capacity for epimorphic regeneration compared to zebrafish. In mice, ear and digit regeneration is impaired by OXPHOS inhibition, while the highly regenerative MRL strain shows increased glycolysis after injury. Disruption of osteoblast metabolic profiles may have implications for bone repair and diseases like osteoporosis, suggesting cell metabolism could be a therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C239-C242 accurately summarize literature on mammalian regeneration (Seifert and Muneoka, 2018; Johnson et al., 2020; Shyh-Chang et al., 2013; Naviaux et al., 2009; Heber-Katz, 2017), noting conflicting results about the role of OXPHOS vs. glycolysis. Claims C243-C244 are speculative about therapeutic applications, though they are grounded in literature about metabolic effects on osteoblast function (Lee et al., 2017; Loeffler et al., 2018; van Gastel and Carmeliet, 2021; Karner and Long, 2018). These represent reasonable extrapolations but lack direct experimental support in this study.

results.result: The study demonstrates that metabolic reprogramming favoring anaerobic glycolysis occurs at early stages of adult regeneration and is an integral component of the regenerative program. This unveils a novel and fundamental role of glycolysis in mediating mature osteoblast dedifferentiation and cell cycle re-entry, uncoupling these processes by identifying distinct downstream transcriptional targets. Glucose metabolism has a powerful instructive role in regulating lineage-specific programs and generic responses to injury that induce changes in cell identity and function.
results.evaluation: Claims C245-C251 provide an appropriate synthesis of the major findings and their significance. The conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental data including transcriptomics (C35-C44), metabolomics (C57-C62), pharmacological manipulations (C77-C90), and mechanistic studies (C91-C121). The claim about uncoupling dedifferentiation from proliferation (C249) is supported by the differential effects of glycolysis inhibition on these processes (C103-C108). The instructive role of metabolism (C251) is supported by the demonstration that glycolysis regulates specific signaling pathways (C99-C101, C111-C112).
